result:
There’s something gentle about being asked to write freely. It feels like being handed an open field with no map, only weather and possibility.

I think I’d write about small thresholds: the moment before sleep when thoughts loosen their grip, the pause between raindrops, the first line of a poem that hasn’t decided what it wants to be yet. So much of life happens in those in-between spaces, where meaning is still soft and unfinished.

Language is strange and beautiful. A word can be ordinary on Monday and devastating by Thursday. “Home,” for instance, begins as a place and ends as a ache. Or “later,” which can mean comfort or avoidance depending on who says it and how quietly.

If I could choose any subject, I’d choose attention itself—the way noticing changes the world. A cracked sidewalk becomes interesting when light falls across it just so. A stranger’s laugh can turn an entire afternoon from gray to gold. Not because the world is different, but because someone has stopped long enough to see it.

Maybe that’s what writing is for: not to explain everything, but to keep the mystery vivid. To say, look—this too exists. This quiet, this flicker, this ordinary miracle.

And if nothing else remains by the end, perhaps one simple thought will: pay attention. The world is speaking, mostly in whispers, and it is worth listening.
